# B2B Healthcare Support

`customer_support.model.b2b.healthcare` · vertical · parent `customer_support.model.b2b`

> Supporting clinical and care-delivery organisations — hospital IT, clinical software, medical device and health data platforms. The defining fact is that a ticket can sit upstream of patient harm, and that changes three things at once. Severity stops being a function of how many users are affected and becomes a function of clinical risk. One clinician unable to see one allergy record outranks an outage affecting a thousand people in a back-office module, and any triage model trained on user counts will get that inversion wrong every time. Diagnosis runs without the data. Patient information cannot travel into a ticket, a log attachment or a screen share, so the reproduction discipline has to be built from de-identified cases and record identifiers rather than from what the customer can see on their screen. The ordinary "send me the failing record" reflex is not merely discouraged here; it creates a breach out of a support gesture. The fix does not arrive when we ship it. Validated environments, change-control boards and release windows mean a hotfix can exist for months before the customer runs it, so the workaround is not a stopgap — it is the thing the clinician will actually use, and it has to be safe enough to be documented as clinical practice. The error carried in from B2B SaaS is pacing the customer against our release calendar. The error carried in from any consumer vertical is optimising for speed of response, when what a clinical customer needs is an answer that is correct and traceable, delivered inside their change process.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a hospital IT analyst or clinical systems administrator; the affected user is a clinician who is mid-shift and will never open a ticket |
| typical_resolution_hours | 48 |
| volume_shape | steady and shift-shaped, with concentrated spikes at go-live, upgrade and integration-rollover events that are scheduled months ahead |
| staffing_model | tiered with clinical-safety review on defect classification, plus a named implementation contact per site |
| coverage | 24x7 for anything touching live clinical workflow, business hours for the rest |
| automation_level | low — deflection is limited by data restrictions and by a user population that cannot experiment on a live system |
| notes | typical_resolution_hours measures time to a safe answer, not time to installed code. The gap between those two is the honest description of this vertical and every metric that hides it is flattering.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `severity`, `priority`, `product_area_ref`


> Severity and priority are both mandatory and both must be set explicitly, because this is the vertical where they invert most often and most expensively. A system that defaults one from the other has silently decided that clinical risk equals user count.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.incident`

Requires `is_customer_visible`, `severity`, `postmortem_required`


> Anything that reached a clinical workflow needs a postmortem regardless of how quickly it was mitigated, because the artefact required afterwards is an assessment of whether harm was possible — not a description of the outage. Deciding that at the end, when the pressure is off and the logs have rotated, is how it stops happening.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `audience`, `verified_against_version`


> Audience is load-bearing because the same procedure written for an IT administrator and for a clinician are different documents with different risks. A downtime workaround written in admin language and handed to a nurse at 3am is a safety problem wearing a documentation problem's clothes.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `severity_assessed`, `receiving_owner_ref`


> The assessed severity, not the perceived one, is what routes here — and it must be recorded separately from what the customer claimed, because the two disagreeing is itself the signal that a clinical-safety review is owed.

> Named regulatory regimes are deliberately absent — clinical safety and privacy obligations differ by country and by whether the product is a regulated device. What is portable is the structure: risk-based severity, diagnosis without patient data, and a fix the customer installs on their calendar rather than ours.
